title: Practice: modal class and median class
intro: Nine questions. For median questions, write the running totals down the side of the table.

hints: Look for the biggest frequency — then give the class, not the number.
questions.explanation: The highest frequency is 16, in $125 \le m < 130$. Answer d gives the frequency itself, which is not a class.

questions.prompt: Complete the running totals for the heights of 30 plants, then use them.
hints: Each running total is the one above plus this row's frequency.
questions.explanation: 4, 12, 23, 30. The median is the $\frac{31}{2} = 15.5$th value. There are 12 values below 30 cm and 23 below 40 cm, so the median lies in $30 \le h < 40$.

questions.prompt: Complete the working for the plant heights.
questions.text: The median lies in position $\frac{30 + 1}{2} =$ [[a]]. There are 12 values smaller than [[b]] cm. The 13th to the 23rd values lie in the class $\square \le h < \square$, so the median class starts at [[c]] and ends at [[d]].
hints: Use the running totals from the last question.
questions.explanation: $15.5$th value. 12 values are below 30 cm, and the next 11 (the 13th to 23rd) are in $30 \le h < 40$, which includes the 15.5th.

questions.prompt: Find the median class one step at a time.

steps.prompt: In which position is the median?
What is the running total after the first **two** classes?
So which class contains the median?
steps.feedback: The 181st to 265th people are in their twenties, and 250.5 is in that range.

questions.explanation: Median position 250.5. Running totals 92, 180, 265 — so the median age is in $20 \le y < 30$, even though the modal class is $0 \le y < 10$.

questions.prompt: Angelique regroups the village ages into $0$–$20$: 180, $20$–$40$: 153, $40$–$60$: 107, $60$–$80$: 60. What is the new modal class?

options.text: It is the same as before

hints: The modal class must be one of the new groups.
questions.explanation: 180 is the highest new frequency, so the modal class is $0 \le y < 20$. The class has changed because the groups have changed — even though the data has not.

questions.prompt: Long jumps (cm): 152, 152, 155, 161, 163, 164, 165, 166, 168, 169, 170, 172, 175, 181, 182. Grouped in tens, the mode of the raw data (152) lies in the modal class.
hints: Count how many jumps are in each group of ten: 150s, 160s, 170s, 180s.
questions.explanation: False. The groups have frequencies 3, 7, 3, 2, so the modal class is $160 \le l < 170$. The raw mode, 152, is in $150 \le l < 160$.

a: 15 is the biggest frequency ✓. b: $\frac{51}{2} = 25.5$ ✓. c: the running total reaches 23 after the third class and 35 after the fourth, so the 25.5th value is in $27 \le t < 31$ ✓ (so e is wrong). d: $39 - 15 = 24$ ✓.

questions.prompt: A histogram shows the ages of 40 people in a sports club: $0$–$10$: 4, $10$–$20$: 9, $20$–$30$: 16, $30$–$40$: 11. Estimate the mean age.
questions.explanation: $\Sigma fx = 940$, $\Sigma f = 40$, so the mean $\approx 23.5$ years.

questions.prompt: This histogram shows 36 exam marks. Increase the frequency of $60 \le x < 80$ so that it becomes the **only** modal class, using the smallest possible number.
hints: The current modal class has a frequency of 12.
questions.explanation: To beat 12 it needs at least 13. (Equal at 12 would give two modal classes.)
